points.quote: VS Code and Theia plugins get one host process per connected frontend. Headless plugins share a single backend host process.

Each plugin runs in a "host process", which is a subprocess the Theia backend spawns. It isolates the plugin from the main process and keeps it from touching Theia services or hurting performance. Browser-side plugins run in web workers

The API is declared in `packages/plugin/src/theia.d.ts`. The implementation is built by `createAPIFactory` in `plugin-ext/src/plugin/plugin-context.ts`. VS Code plugins import `vscode`. The override is in `plugin-ext-vscode/src/node/plugin-vscode-init.ts`.

Node hosts override module loading so the plugin can import that object: Theia plugins import `@theia/plugin`... VS Code plugins import `vscode`... In web workers, the API is assigned to `window['theia']`.
Each side holds an RPC proxy of the other side's interface. Both interfaces are defined in `plugin-ext/src/common/plugin-api-rpc.ts`... Methods callable over RPC start with `$`.
VS Code and Theia plugins get one host process per connected frontend... plugin host ↔ Theia backend ↔ browser. The backend only relays messages.
By default it encodes with msgpackr... Functions and object references don't [cross]. For a provider with callbacks, the creating side caches the object and sends a handle, usually an id.
Headless plugins share a single backend host process... their Main side runs in the node backend... They only see custom APIs that the application or other headless plugins contribute.
